name: Sclerotherapy

lead: Sclerotherapy is a procedure in which a clinician injects a sclerosing solution into small veins so they shrink, scar and are absorbed by the body. It is used to treat spider veins (telangiectasias) and small varicose veins, which makes legs look clearer and more even.

A 2017 review describes cosmetic sclerotherapy as a frequently used, low-risk and highly successful method for these veins. Wikipedia describes it as considered the gold standard for large spider veins, usually needing at least two sessions several weeks apart.

paras: Treatment takes around 10 minutes per session, with a clinician injecting the agent, often polidocanol or sodium tetradecyl sulfate, sometimes as a foam. Patients typically wear compression stockings or bandages for about a week and are encouraged to walk. Veins fade over weeks.

Reported complications include hyperpigmentation, redness, thrombophlebitis, allergic reaction and, rarely, clots, visual disturbances and skin necrosis if the agent leaks outside the vein. Tamoxifen use and known allergy to the agent are contraindications. Foam has raised questions about bubbles reaching the heart, lungs and brain, though large studies consider it safe.

chain: Vein closes, scars and is absorbed
Fewer visible veins, more even-looking legs
angle.text: The injection eliminates the visible veins themselves, so the skin over them looks clearer. It is a clinic procedure used for cosmetic vein concerns.

lead: Sclerotherapy involves injecting a fluid into blood vessels to eradicate them [1]. In adults it treats spider veins, smaller varicose veins, hemorrhoids and hydroceles, and it is also used for vascular and lymphatic malformations [2]. In appearance terms, the use is cosmetic: closing visible spider and reticular veins on the legs.

A 2017 review calls telangiectasias and spider veins a common cosmetic concern for both women and men and describes sclerotherapy as a frequently used, low-risk and highly successful method [3]. Wikipedia states that it is considered the gold standard for large spider veins and also closes the reticular feeder veins under the skin, which makes recurrence less likely [2].
The treated vein first shrinks from muscle spasm, then scars and is absorbed over weeks [2]. Most people need at least two sessions several weeks apart [2].
infobox: Polidocanol, sodium tetradecyl sulfate, foam forms
Spider veins, reticular veins, small varicose veins
Compression stockings or bandages for about a week
Usually at least two, weeks apart

paras: A sclerosing agent is injected into the vein, which causes it to shrink and then gradually scar closed and be absorbed [2]. Agents include sodium tetradecyl sulfate, developed in 1946 and still widely used, and polidocanol in liquid, foam and microfoam forms [2]. Foam displaces blood and stays in contact with the vein wall, which makes it more effective on larger and longer veins [2]. Larger veins can be treated with ultrasound guidance [2]. The procedure takes about 10 minutes, with minimal downtime and a week or so of compression [2].

The first recorded attempt was in 1682 using an acid, and nineteenth-century agents such as iron perchlorate led to side effects and near abandonment by 1894 [2]. George Fegan's work in the 1960s, duplex ultrasound in the 1980s and foam techniques from the 1990s advanced the method [2].

Wikipedia reports that a Cochrane review concluded sclerotherapy's place in modern practice is usually limited to recurrent varicose veins after surgery and thread veins, and that other reviews found surgery or endovenous ablation superior for veins with saphenous junction reflux [2]. For cosmetic spider veins, a 2023 randomized trial compared sclerotherapy with radiofrequency thermocoagulation [4]. Clinical practice guidelines from vascular surgery societies address varicose vein management more broadly [5][6].

Rare complications include venous thromboembolism, visual disturbances, allergic reaction, thrombophlebitis, skin necrosis, hyperpigmentation and redness [2]. If the agent leaks outside the vein, tissue necrosis and scarring can occur [2]. One stroke has been reported after an unusually large foam volume, and the significance of small bubbles reaching the heart, lungs and brain is not fully understood, although large studies consider foam sclerotherapy safe [2]. The 2017 cosmetic review describes complications and follow-up care [3].

Studies include a 2017 review of cosmetic sclerotherapy [3], a 2024 Phlebology article on microsclerotherapy [7], a 2023 randomized trial comparing sclerotherapy with radiofrequency thermocoagulation for spider veins [4], and a 2026 randomized trial comparing 3% polidocanol foam with saline prewashing against standard foam for varicose veins [8]. Society guidelines on varicose veins were published in 2022 and 2023 [5][6].
